title: The Brightest Room
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 30 of 40
content:
The brightest room in town had been dark for years, and Greg volunteered us before asking whether I liked volunteering. The reopened community center had its own weather, noises, and opinion about whether I was prepared. I stood in the middle of it with the kind of courage that appears after a person has already said yes. The reflex to run had not vanished because love became possible. It had simply lost the argument for the morning.

The plan was to turn an empty building into a place where people could make things together. Greg wrote it on a receipt, then copied it onto cleaner paper when he decided the first version looked too much like a confession. Nothing was complicated, which made it frightening. Complicated plans came with exits. This one asked us to notice what we were building while we were building it. I kept my hands busy with painted walls, buzzing lights, and chairs scraping into a circle and tried not to count the ways a good day could become a test.

Greg arrived with one joke already spent and another held in reserve. He was good at making a room less sharp. He was also good at hiding the bruise beneath the joke if nobody asked him to stop. He negotiated with a smile until the smile disappeared, then defended art as more than decoration. When he looked at me, the familiar warmth was there, along with the question he was trying not to ask: was I staying because I wanted him, or because I had grown used to being wanted?

I answered by taking an active part in the mess. I took the budget sheets, asked hard questions, and refused to copy his methods. It mattered to do something that could not be mistaken for passive trust. Greg made space for people so generously that they could forget he needed space too. I did not want to accept his care as an endless resource. I wanted to meet him in the middle, where a hand could be offered and still be allowed to pull back.

The complication was already there: a donor wanted control over the program in exchange for money. It was not a disaster. Beach City produced problems small enough to laugh at and serious enough to reveal a person. Greg's shoulders tightened. His instinct was to fix the practical thing first, then ask whether anyone had feelings about it. I caught his wrist before he disappeared into the task. He looked down at my hand as if I had interrupted a song.

We talked about his old guitar pick in my coat pocket. The object was ordinary when it entered our lives, but ordinary things collected meaning when we returned to them. Greg told the story again, leaving out the version where he made himself the fool. He had been young, lonely, and brave in ways he did not know how to name. I was not interested in punishing the person he had been. I was interested in the person beside me now, still learning how to ask.

“A room becomes welcoming when people may change its arrangement.” Greg said, embarrassed by the wisdom of his own sentence.

We took a break without calling it one. Greg found something cold to drink, and I sat where I could see the work waiting for us without being swallowed by it. He told me three small stories about painted walls, buzzing lights, and chairs scraping into a circle: one funny, one embarrassing, and one that ended with him admitting he had been scared. I answered with a truth of my own. The exchange was not dramatic enough for a song, which was exactly why it mattered. Real intimacy kept happening in the unlit spaces between declarations. I could be tired and still be wanted. Greg could be uncertain and still be someone I trusted. We did not have to turn every feeling into a performance before it counted.

I told him what I wanted next. Greg accepted my leadership instead of turning every task into his rescue mission. Greg did not rush to reassure me. He did not promise never to fail or never to need more than I could give. He promised to tell me when fear was driving. That was better. A perfect man would have been a stranger. Greg was a person with a van, a guitar, a history of running, and a stubborn desire to come home honestly.

We danced under the work lights and kissed against the paint-smelling wall. The room could wait until morning.

The room was unfinished, but its windows were lit from inside. We looked at the paint on our hands and called it a beginning.

bridge_outro: At the Lanternwell's winter gathering, Greg played a song nobody had asked him to make perfect. Katara helped the children hang paper stars; Iroh kept the tea hot; Severus stood near the edge of the crowd and pretended not to recognize the melody by its second refrain. Greg caught me looking at him and waggled his eyebrows until I laughed. Later, when the square emptied, he admitted that being heard without needing to impress anyone still frightened him. We walked to Starwake Pier together. He did not fill the silence with another song. I was grateful he knew I could love the person who remained when the music stopped.
